title: Louisiana Act 810 NIL Consent Checklist
tagline: What should be in writing before anyone uses a minor's name, image, or likeness in Louisiana.
description: A family-use checklist for Louisiana Act 810 NIL consent: who signs, what the written consent should cover, and what good records look like.
intro: Act 810 governs name, image, and likeness (NIL) rights in Louisiana. Before a minor's image appears in a highlight, a sponsorship post, or a clinic video, written consent needs to exist. This one-page checklist walks families through the decision points so consent is explicit, dated, and documented.
bullets: Who must sign: consent typically involves the parent or guardian and the minor
What the consent covers: the purpose of use, channels, duration, and any compensation terms
What records to keep: signed copies, dates, and the platform or use each consent applies to
When to revisit: after a transfer, a birthday, or a change in who controls the account
Education first: this checklist is guidance, not legal advice; a lawyer should review final documents whenever money is involved

title: Verify Your Would-Be Sports Agent
tagline: A simple pre-signing checklist for families and student-athletes.
description: How to verify someone who claims to be a sports agent before signing anything: registration, credentials, written terms, and red flags.
intro: Louisiana regulates athlete agents through the Representing Athletes Act (La. R.S. 51:2500 et seq.). Before a family signs any agreement, someone claiming to represent an athlete should be registered, verifiable, and willing to put every term in writing.
bullets: Confirm the person is a registered sports agent for your state, or an attorney in good standing
Ask who licenses or registers them and how to verify it - then verify it yourself
Get every scope, fee, and expense term in a signed written agreement
Do not sign under time pressure or before conflicts of interest are disclosed
An 'education, not representation' consultant should say so in writing and never hold themselves out as an agent
Red flags: guaranteed outcomes, cash-upfront demands, or eligibility treated as an afterthought

title: Master vs. Sync vs. Neighboring Rights
tagline: Three rights in one song - and who gets paid for each.
description: A one-page reference on the difference between a master recording, synchronization (sync), and neighboring rights in music.
intro: A single song contains multiple rights. In highlight reels, event content, and social video, schools and creators routinely need more than one permission. This reference untangles the three most common rights so the next clearance question is clear.
bullets: Master: the actual sound recording and who owns that file
Sync: the right to pair music with moving images - required for any video using a song
Neighboring rights: performance-side royalties tied to the recording, adjacent to copyright
Highlight reels usually need both master and sync clearance; buying the song does not grant sync rights
When in doubt, treat unlicensed music in video as a clearance question, not a taste question

title: What to Record Before Your First Production Deal
tagline: A template for producers, artists, and families entering a first production agreement.
description: A structured template for documenting the essentials of a first production deal: scope, credit, ownership, payments, and delivery.
intro: The most common creative-production disputes start with what nobody wrote down. Before work begins, producers and artists should agree on scope, credit, ownership, payment, and delivery - in writing. This template keeps the conversation to one page and makes the next session productive.
bullets: Parties: legal names, not stage names or handles
Scope: recordings or beats, deliverables, and how many revisions are included
Credit: how each side is credited in titles, metadata, and social posts
Ownership: who owns the master and the underlying composition rights
Payment: amounts, timing, and what event triggers each payment
Delivery: file formats, stems, masters, and deadlines

title: Should Families Brand Kids Early?
tagline: The one-page version of a longer essay.
description: A short decision aid for families weighing early sports branding: what to build, what to skip, and who controls the account.
intro: Branding a young athlete early is not inherently good or bad. It is a decision about control, records, and consent. This one-pager gives families a simple lens: build evidence, not hype, and keep the family in control of every account and asset.
bullets: Build documentation of results - times, tests, highlights - before chasing followers
Keep account ownership and passwords with the parent or guardian
Put written consent in place before posting minors (see the Act 810 checklist)
Avoid 'manager' or 'agent' labels unless someone is genuinely registered and licensed for that role
Read the longer essay on the blog: Should Families Brand Kids Early?

title: Podcast Episode One-Sheet Template

intro: A one-sheet is the fastest way to explain a podcast episode to a potential sponsor or guest. This template keeps it to one page: who, why, for whom, and what they get from joining.

Guest or topic value in two sentences

One contact route so every inquiry lands in the same place

title: Brand, Music & NIL Glossary
tagline: Plain-English definitions for the terms people throw around.
description: A reference glossary covering brand, music, NIL, and media IP terms used across jaylensinegal.com.
intro: Terms like sync, master, NIL, and fair use get tossed around quickly. This glossary keeps a plain-English reference for families, schools, and creators. It is an educational aid, not a set of legal definitions.
bullets: NIL: name, image, and likeness - the rights tied to a person's identity in commercial use
Act 810: Louisiana's state law framework for NIL consent
Master: the sound recording file and who owns it
Sync license: permission to pair a song with moving images
Neighboring rights: performance royalties tied to a recording
Fair use: a limited defense for using copyrighted material; it is not a blanket permission
DMCA: the US statute that provides safe-harbor workflows for online content
Hudl: a sports media platform; check its terms before assuming you own your highlights
Platform lock-in: losing control of your content because the platform keeps it
